notes.title: Chapter map: Packaging, environments & tooling
notes.html:
How code gets found (63, 64), installed (65, 66) and checked (67). Read each arrow as a sentence: import machinery built on the import system.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order: 63 import system ─▶ 64 import machinery ─▶ 65 venvs & resolution ─▶ 66 packaging ─▶ 67 testing & tooling

🌳 Which dependency workflow?

The tools in 65 are alternatives for one job, so the choice lives here (moved from note 65).

What each leaf is, and the one condition that would change the answer:

  • ⚡ uv run --with (venvs): if the script gets shared or scheduled, give it a project and a lock.

  • 🧰 pip + venv (venvs): if two installs ever disagree, you needed a lock; the first "works on my machine" is the signal.

  • 🚀 uv project (venvs): if the organisation mandates the PEP 751 pylock.toml format, export to it rather than switching tools.

  • 📜 Poetry (packaging): if resolver speed hurts CI, uv reads the same pyproject.toml intent.

  • 🧩 pip-tools (venvs): if you also need building and publishing, add a build backend rather than a second resolver.

  • The one big idea: every tool here separates intent from resolution: imports resolve names through a cache, environments resolve versions into a lock, and tests resolve fixtures by name; reproducibility comes from recording the resolution.

  • The two most-confused pairs: import m vs from m import name (63: use-time vs import-time lookup, which also decides where to patch in 67) · requirements vs lockfile (65: intent vs solution).

  • Ten minutes before an interview: 63's circular-import sequence diagram, 65's resolver flowchart, 67's fixture-resolution flowchart.

  • Cross-chapter: names & binding (import is a binding statement) · generators (yield fixtures) · multiprocessing (spawn re-imports your module).

notes.title: The Import System
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 The import system · 📘 The module cache · 📘 __main__: top-level code · 📘 importlib

⚡ TL;DR

import checks sys.modules; on a miss it finds the module, registers it before running its body, runs the body, then binds a name. Registration-before-execution makes imports idempotent and circular imports "work" until something touches a half-built module.

🧭 Flow: import m ─▶ sys.modules["m"] hit? bind it, done ─▶ miss: finders on sys.meta_path return a spec ─▶ create an empty module ─▶ insert into sys.modules NOW ─▶ execute the body top to bottom ─▶ bind the name in the importer ─▶ body raised? evict the entry

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What makes import idempotent? The sys.modules cache: the first import executes the module; later ones are a dict lookup.
When does a module enter sys.modules? Before its body executes, which is why a cycle sees a half-initialized module.
Why does from m import name fail in a cycle when import m survives? from reads the attribute at import time; import m defers the lookup to use time.
What does if __name__ == "__main__": test? Whether this module is the process entry point ("__main__") or was imported (its dotted name).
What is from . import x resolved against? The package in __package__, which is unset when the file runs as a script.
✏️ Draw by hand: the cycle models registered ─▶ imports services ─▶ services gets cached half-built models ─▶ models.User at top level ─▶ AttributeError.

💡 The idea

A module is executed once, and every later import gets the same object: that's why module-level state is a process-wide singleton. The ordering detail is what interviews probe. Two modules that import each other, on CPython 3.12:

# models.py                         # services.py
import services                     import models          # cache hit: half-built
class User: ...                     first = models.User    # runs NOW

$ python -c "import models"
AttributeError: partially initialized module 'models' has no attribute 'User'
(most likely due to a circular import)

models was in sys.modules before its body ran, so services got it from the cache instead of recursing, but class User hadn't executed yet. A function body that says models.User is fine, because that lookup happens at call time, when both modules are complete. The cycle isn't the crash; module-level access during the cycle is.

The trade: one cache makes imports cheap, idempotent and safe in cycles, and in exchange a module can be observed half-built, so module-level code must not lean on its importers.

⚙️ How it works

The algorithm for one import:

The cycle from The idea, step by step (markers match the Code section):

Rule What actually happens
Binding import a.b binds a; from a import b copies the current binding of b into your namespace, which is why mocks must patch where a name is used, not where it's defined.
Packages Importing myapp executes myapp/__init__.py, so a heavy __init__ taxes every importer, and re-exports there create import-order coupling.
Scripts vs -m python pkg/tool.py has no package context: from . import sib gave ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package; python -m pkg.tool worked.
Thread safety A per-module import lock means two threads importing one module never execute it twice.

💻 Code

The cycle annotated, and the fixes in order of preference:

# models.py: the entry point imports this FIRST
import services                    # ① models is registered and half-built
class User:                        #   defined only AFTER services.py finishes
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name

# services.py
import models                      # ② cache HIT: the half-initialized models
def make_user():                   # ③ models.User is looked up at CALL time: safe
    return models.User("prabha")
first = models.User                # ④ ❌ module-level access runs NOW → AttributeError
                                   # ⑤ both entries are evicted; the error unwinds into models

# Fixes, best first:
#  1. restructure: move User to a third module both import (cycles are a layering smell)
#  2. defer: import inside the function that needs it (one dict lookup per call)
#  3. weaken: `import models` + `models.User` at use time, never `from models import User`
#  4. typing-only cycles: `if TYPE_CHECKING:` imports + string annotations

Reordering statements until the cycle "happens to work" is load-bearing luck: the next added line breaks it. from m2 import User in the same shape fails louder, with ImportError: cannot import name 'User' from partially initialized module 'm2'.

⚠️ Break it: side effects at import time.

# util.py, imported by every entry point
import torch                       # ❌ heavy optional dependency at module level
CLIENT = make_db_client()          # ❌ a connection opened by merely importing
# look for: `python -X importtime -c "import util"` puts torch at the top
# naive model predicts: imports are free; the work happens when you call something

Import time is cold-start latency: every worker, Lambda cold start, CLI call and pytest session pays the whole transitive graph first. -X importtime prints per-module microseconds (json took 6.2 ms cumulative here) and names the culprit line; the fix is a function-local import at the point of use.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: import checks sys.modules; on a miss it finds and loads the module, then binds a name. The critical detail is order: the empty module goes into sys.modules before its body runs. That makes imports idempotent and lets circular imports work, because the second importer gets a cache hit on a half-initialized module. It fails only when something touches an attribute not defined yet, which is why from x import name is the classic trigger and import x usually survives.

Q · Mechanism — Walk through import myapp.services, statement to bound name. Check sys.modules["myapp.services"]; a hit binds immediately. On a miss, import the parent myapp first, recursively. Ask the sys.meta_path finders for a spec: the path finder walks myapp.__path__ for services.py or services/__init__.py (import machinery). The loader creates an empty module, inserts it into sys.modules immediately, then executes the body. Finally the name is bound: myapp for import myapp.services. If the body raises, the entry is evicted so a retry re-executes.

Q · Failure — After a refactor, startup dies with cannot import name 'User' from partially initialized module. What happened, and which fix first? Someone created a cycle: models imports services at the top, and services does from models import User at the top, so it cache-hits a models that never got past its first line. Fix by preference: restructure (extract the shared type downward), defer the import into the function, switch to import models with use-time lookup, and TYPE_CHECKING for typing-only cycles. Reordering lines isn't a fix. Then add an import-linter contract so the cycle can't return.

Q · Design — Startup for a large FastAPI service: fast imports, no cycles, heavy optional deps off the common path. Module level holds definitions only; connections, clients and model loading live in lifespan hooks or explicit init(). Heavy optional imports (torch, pandas) are deferred into the handlers or subcommands that need them. Enforce a one-way layering, schemas → services → api, with import-linter in CI, plus a startup budget test running python -X importtime -c "import app". It breaks by creep: a transitive dependency starts importing pandas at module level. I'd watch cold-start p99 per release.

⚖️ Compare

import m from m import name from . import m
Binds the module object one attribute, copied a sibling via the current package
Attribute resolved at use time at import time at import time
In a cycle usually survives the classic trigger same trigger as from
Breaks when rarely the name isn't defined yet the file runs as a script

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Circular imports are always an error"
    ✅ Cycles that only reference each other lazily run fine; module-level access fails.
    ↳ Worse: it works until someone adds one line.
  • 🪞 "from m import f gives me a live view of m.f"
    ✅ It copies the binding at import time.
    ↳ So: patch where the name is used, not where it's defined.
  • ❌ "__init__.py is just an empty marker"
    ✅ It's the package's module body, run on first import; its absence makes a namespace package.
  • 🔀 Not the same as running a file
    ↳ Difference: python file.py has no package context; python -m pkg.mod does, so relative imports work.
  • ⚠️ Don't mutate sys.path in application code.
    ↳ Why: resolution then depends on the working directory; that's a packaging problem.
  • ⚠️ Don't use importlib.reload in services.
    ↳ Why: names other modules copied with from still point at the old objects. Restart instead.
  • 🔖 Version: semantics stable since 3.3 (per-module import locks); "partially initialized" wording 3.8+; -P / PYTHONSAFEPATH 3.11+ stops prepending the script's directory to sys.path.
    ↳ Note: checked on CPython 3.12.13.

🕸️ Connections

Path: names & binding ─▶ import system ─▶ import machinery ─▶ packaging

  • Builds on names & binding: import is a binding statement; module object vs name is the whole story.
  • Used by testing: mock.patch targets import paths, and from-imports decide where to patch.
  • Breaks when combined with multiprocessing: spawn re-imports your module, so unguarded top-level code runs again in every child.
  • Contrasts with import machinery: this note is the algorithm; that one is the pluggable finders and loaders under the "find" step.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Node's CommonJS require also caches before executing, and returns a partially filled exports object in a cycle.

notes.title: Import Machinery Internals
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 importlib: the implementation of import · 📜 PEP 420: namespace packages

⚡ TL;DR

Import is a pluggable protocol: finders on sys.meta_path return a spec, and the spec's loader executes the module. sys.path order decides shadowing, and sys.path[0] is the script's directory, so a local logging.py beats the stdlib.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Finder vs loader? A finder locates a module and returns a spec; the spec's loader executes it.
The sys.path[0] gotcha? It's the script's directory, prepended, so local files shadow the stdlib. -P (3.11+) disables it.
Namespace package? A package with no __init__.py, assembled from several sys.path locations (PEP 420).

💡 The idea

The import algorithm's "find" step asks sys.meta_path in order: BuiltinImporter, FrozenImporter, then PathFinder, which searches sys.path and caches per-directory results in sys.path_importer_cache. Because the protocol is pluggable, zip imports, PyInstaller and pytest's assertion rewriting are just extra finders. Because sys.path order decides who wins, a local logging.py silently replaces the stdlib for every import in that process. PYTHONPATH hacks reorder this globally and invisibly; packaging fixes what path hacks patch.

💻 Code

import sys, importlib.util
print(sys.meta_path)                             # BuiltinImporter, FrozenImporter, PathFinder
spec = importlib.util.find_spec("json")
print(spec.origin, spec.loader)                  # where it lives, and what will execute it
print(importlib.util.find_spec("logging").origin)  # WHICH file will `import logging` run?
# CPython 3.12, with a logging.py beside the script → …/shadow/logging.py  (your bug)
# same script under `python -P`                    → …/lib/python3.12/logging/__init__.py

notes.title: Virtual Environments & Dependency Resolution
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 venv · 📘 pip: dependency resolution · 📘 uv docs

⚡ TL;DR

A venv is a pyvenv.cfg plus its own site-packages: it redirects sys.prefix, and nothing is copied. The hard part is resolution: one version per package for the whole environment, so keep intent and the resolved lock as separate files.

🧭 Flow: humans edit loose intent in pyproject.toml ─▶ resolver picks one version per package meeting every transitive constraint ─▶ conflict? backtrack and retry older candidates ─▶ solution written to a lockfile with hashes ─▶ CI and prod install exactly the lock, no resolving

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a venv actually change? sys.prefix, via pyvenv.cfg: its own site-packages, the base interpreter's binary and stdlib.
requirements.txt vs a lockfile? Requirements are intent (loose constraints); a lock is the solution (every transitive dependency pinned and hashed).
Why can pip install spend minutes "resolving"? Backtracking: a wrong guess deep in the tree forces discarding candidates and retrying.

💡 The idea

Activation is cosmetic: it prepends the venv's bin/ to PATH. The real mechanism runs at interpreter startup, on CPython 3.12:

# .venv/pyvenv.cfg →  home = …/cpython-3.12-macos-aarch64-none/bin
import sys
sys.prefix              # …/.venv: where site-packages comes from
sys.base_prefix         # …/cpython-3.12.13-…: where the stdlib comes from
sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix   # True: the canonical "am I in a venv?" check

.venv/bin/python is a symlink to the base interpreter, which finds pyvenv.cfg beside itself. So calling it directly equals activating (what Dockerfiles, systemd units and CI do), and deleting the base Python bricks every venv built from it. Copying a venv to another path breaks too: scripts hardcode absolute shebangs. Because Python allows only one version of a package per environment, two dependencies wanting incompatible versions of a third is a real conflict, and the resolver's job is to find one assignment that satisfies everything.

The trade: a flat, single-version environment keeps imports simple, and in exchange resolution is a search that can be slow or impossible, so you record its answer instead of re-solving it.

⚙️ How it works

Loose requirements are re-solved on every install, so today's environment differs from last month's the moment any transitive dependency releases. A lock skips resolution and verifies hashes: same input, same bytes, plus tamper detection. Which tool owns that loop is a choice in the chapter map.

💻 Code

The reproducibility loop, with uv:

uv add "httpx>=0.27"     # edits pyproject.toml (intent) AND re-locks uv.lock (solution)
uv lock --upgrade-package httpx   # deliberate upgrade: the lock diff is the review
uv sync --frozen         # CI and prod: install EXACTLY the lock; fail if it drifted
uv run --with rich python script.py   # throwaway script: no project pollution
# Never `pip install pkg` ad hoc into a locked project: that's unrecorded drift.

The two-file discipline is what code review needs: edit intent, regenerate the lock, commit both, and the lock diff is the dependency change.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A venv is an isolated site-packages selected by pyvenv.cfg and sys.prefix: cheap, disposable, one per project. Resolution is the hard part: pip's backtracking resolver must find one version of every package satisfying all transitive constraints, because an environment holds one version per package. So humans edit loose constraints in pyproject.toml, a tool generates a lockfile with exact versions and hashes, and CI installs only from the lock.

Q · Mechanism — Why isn't pip install -r requirements.txt reproducible, and what makes a lockfile different? Loose pins (requests>=2.28) are a constraint set solved fresh each time, and even pinned top-level requirements leave transitives floating unless you froze them all. pip freeze photographs an environment, including stale and dev-only packages, with no hashes and no link to intent. A lock is the recorded solution derived from intent (uv lock, poetry lock, pip-compile): every package, exact version, artifact hashes. Installs from it skip resolution and verify bytes.

⚖️ Compare

Tool What it is Lock Reach for it when
pip + venv installer + isolation pip freeze (a snapshot, not a derivation) minimal deps, base images
pip-tools pip-compile: intent → pinned requirements ✅ compiled requirements.txt locking with no new workflow
Poetry project manager: build, publish, lock ✅ poetry.lock one tool owning packaging and deps
uv Rust-fast pip, pip-tools, venv and project manager ✅ uv.lock the 2026 default: 10–100× faster installs

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "A venv is a copy of Python"
    ✅ It's a config file plus an empty site-packages; the binary and stdlib stay in the base install.
  • ❌ "pip freeze > requirements.txt gives reproducible builds"
    ✅ It snapshots whatever is installed, with no hashes and no link to intent.
  • ⚠️ Don't install into the system interpreter.
    ↳ Why: one shared site-packages guarantees conflicts and can break OS tools (PEP 668's externally-managed-environment refusal).
  • ⚠️ Don't ship a venv as an artifact.
    ↳ Why: absolute shebangs and pyvenv.cfg paths break on another machine; rebuild from the lock, which is the artifact.
  • ⚠️ Don't hand-pin transitive deps to fix one conflict.
    ↳ Why: you've become a manual resolver without hashes; regenerate the lock from intent.
  • 🔖 Version: pip's backtracking resolver since pip 20.3; PEP 751 standardizes a pylock.toml lock format, with tool support still rolling out.
    ↳ Note: venv behaviour checked with uv 0.11 on CPython 3.12.13.

🕸️ Connections

Path: import system ─▶ venvs & resolution ─▶ packaging

  • Builds on import machinery: sys.prefix → site-packages → sys.path is how a venv changes what import finds.
  • Used by packaging: the same pyproject.toml declares dependency intent and your package's build.
  • Used by testing: CI correctness starts with --frozen installs; "flaky env" failures are usually resolution drift.
  • Same idea elsewhere: npm's package.json + package-lock.json and Cargo's Cargo.toml + Cargo.lock split intent from solution the same way.

notes.title: Packaging & Distribution
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Writing your pyproject.toml · 📘 Packaging Python projects

⚡ TL;DR

One pyproject.toml declares metadata, dependencies and a build backend that produces two artifacts: sdists and wheels. A wheel is prebuilt, so install is just unpacking; entry points turn python path/to/script.py into a real command.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Wheel vs sdist? Wheel: a prebuilt zip, install is unpack. Sdist: source that needs a build step, maybe a compiler, at install time.
Build backend? The tool [build-system] names to turn source into artifacts (setuptools, hatchling, maturin); pip, uv and build just call it.
Entry point? [project.scripts] maps cli-name = "pkg.mod:func"; the installer generates the executable.

💡 The idea

PEP 517 decouples frontend from backend, so pip, uv or python -m build can drive any backend; a wheel is why pip install numpy needs no compiler. Entry points also kill the relative-import-in-scripts problem, since the command runs your code as an installed package (import system). Dependencies here are abstract intent (httpx>=0.27); the lockfile pins them. Internal code deserves the same treatment: package it, version it, install it, even if "publishing" means a private index.

💻 Code

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]                 # what the frontend installs to build you
build-backend = "hatchling.build"        # who produces the wheel and sdist

[project]
name = "algo-toolkit"
version = "0.3.0"
dependencies = ["httpx>=0.27"]           # intent; the lockfile pins it

[project.scripts]
algo = "algo_toolkit.cli:main"           # installs an `algo` command on PATH
# `uv build` → algo_toolkit-0.3.0-py2.py3-none-any.whl + algo_toolkit-0.3.0.tar.gz;
# the wheel's entry_points.txt holds [console_scripts] algo = algo_toolkit.cli:main

notes.title: Testing & Quality Tooling
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 pytest: how to use fixtures · 📘 unittest.mock · 📘 pytest: parametrize

⚡ TL;DR

pytest injects fixtures by parameter name, resolving a dependency graph with per-scope caching and teardown after yield. The number-one mocking rule: patch where a name is used, not where it's defined.

🧭 Flow: def test_login(client, db) ─▶ match each parameter name to a fixture (nearest conftest.py wins) ─▶ resolve that fixture's own parameters first ─▶ reuse it if cached for its scope ─▶ run up to yield, inject, run the test ─▶ teardown after yield, in reverse order, even on failure

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
How does pytest inject a fixture? By name: the parameter is matched to a registered fixture; the graph resolves recursively, cached per scope.
The number-one mock.patch rule? Patch where the name is used: a from-import copied the binding into the consumer.
Fixture scopes? function (default), class, module, package, session: wider is faster but shares mutable state.

💡 The idea

A mock that "isn't taking effect" is the most common Python testing bug, and it's the import system's from-import copy in disguise. With pytest on CPython 3.12:

# payments.py
def stripe_charge(amount): raise RuntimeError("REAL API CALLED")
# checkout.py
from payments import stripe_charge          # copies the binding into checkout
def pay(amount): return stripe_charge(amount)

# test_pay.py
def test_patch_where_defined():
    with mock.patch("payments.stripe_charge", return_value="ok"):
        assert checkout.pay(10) == "ok"     # → RuntimeError: REAL API CALLED
def test_patch_where_used():
    with mock.patch("checkout.stripe_charge", return_value="ok") as m:
        assert checkout.pay(10) == "ok"     # passes
    m.assert_called_once_with(10)

The first patch rebound payments.stripe_charge, a room nobody looks in; checkout still held the original. Patch the consumer's copy, or have checkout use import payments so there's one live binding. Better still, inject the client and nothing needs patching.

The trade: fixtures and patching make setup composable and dependencies swappable, and in exchange tests couple to import paths and scopes, so a careless patch or a wide scope gives tests that lie.

⚙️ How it works

How pytest resolves def test_login(client, db):

Rule What actually happens
Lookup order The test module, conftest.py files up the tree, then plugins; the nearest definition wins.
Teardown A yield fixture is a generator: code after yield runs even when the test fails, which is why it replaced setUp/tearDown pairs.
Assert rewriting pytest rewrites assert at import time through its own import hook, so a failure shows the operand values.

💻 Code

import pytest
from checkout import price_with_tax

@pytest.fixture
def fx_rates(monkeypatch):                    # composes with the built-in monkeypatch
    monkeypatch.setattr("checkout.fetch_rates", lambda: {"IN": 0.18})  # where USED
    yield                                     # the test runs here
    # monkeypatch undoes itself after yield: no manual teardown

@pytest.mark.parametrize(("amount", "expected"), [
    (100.0, 118.0),
    (0.0, 0.0),                               # the boundary rides the same body
])
def test_price_with_tax(fx_rates, amount, expected):
    assert price_with_tax(amount, region="IN") == pytest.approx(expected)

Around the tests sits the merge gate: ruff (lint and format), mypy or pyright (types), and pytest --cov with branch coverage, all installed from a frozen lock so the gate is reproducible.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: pytest's core idea is dependency injection by name: a test declares parameters, and pytest resolves each against the fixture graph, recursively, with per-scope caching, so setup composes (db → session → user). parametrize runs one body over a case table. monkeypatch and mock.patch swap dependencies with automatic undo; the classic bug is patching where a name is defined instead of where it's used. Around it: ruff, a type checker and coverage as the CI gate.

Q · Mechanism — The team's mock "isn't taking effect": the real API still gets called. Diagnose it. mock.patch("payments.stripe_charge") replaces the attribute on the module named in the string. If checkout.py did from payments import stripe_charge, it copied the binding at import time, so patching payments rebinds an attribute checkout no longer reads. Fix: mock.patch("checkout.stripe_charge"), or import payments in checkout for one live binding. Architecturally, inject the client instead of using a module-level global; injected dependencies need no patching.

⚖️ Compare

pytest unittest
Setup fixture DI graph, scoped caching setUp/tearDown, inheritance
Assertions plain assert, rewritten to show values self.assertEqual family
Parametrization first-class parametrize subTest, weaker isolation
Pick when the default for apps and libraries no dependencies allowed; legacy suites

🚫 Pitfalls

  • 🔀 Not the same: monkeypatch vs mock.patch
    ↳ Difference: monkeypatch replaces attributes, env vars and paths with auto-undo; mock.patch also hands you a Mock to interrogate (assert_called_once_with).
  • 🪞 "Fixtures run once per test file"
    ✅ Scope decides; the default is once per test function.
    ↳ And: a session fixture returning a mutable dict is a hidden global.
  • ⚠️ Don't over-mock.
    ↳ Why: a test that mocks every collaborator verifies the mocks; mock at process boundaries (network, clock, filesystem).
  • ⚠️ Don't widen fixture scope for speed without checking mutability.
    ↳ Why: tests couple through shared state and fail by execution order, then vanish under -x or xdist.
  • ⚠️ Don't chase 100% coverage.
    ↳ Why: coverage measures execution, not assertion; a branch-coverage threshold catches regressions.
  • ⚠️ Don't time.sleep in async or concurrent tests.
    ↳ Why: flaky by construction; inject a clock or await a real completion signal.

🕸️ Connections

Path: import system ─▶ testing ─▶ structured logging

  • Builds on the import system: patch-where-used follows from from-import binding copies.
  • Builds on generators: yield fixtures are generators; teardown is resuming them.
  • Builds on venvs & locks: a reproducible gate needs --frozen installs.
  • Contrasts with protocols: an injected fake that fits a Protocol needs no patching at all.
  • Same idea elsewhere: JUnit 5 injects parameters by type and Spring's test context caches beans per context, the same DI-plus-scope idea.
